rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Phosphine is ammonia's sickly, dangerous cousin. Prepared by heating white phosphorus with concentrated NaOH (**P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂**) or hydrolysing Ca₃P₂, it is a colourless garlic-smelling poison, pyramidal at **93.6°** (nearly pure p-bonding), with a tiny dipole (0.58 D) and a low boiling point (−87.7 °C — no hydrogen bonding).…

rows.text: - P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂ - Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃ - PH₄I + NaOH → PH₃ + NaI + H₂O - PH₃ + HBr → PH₄Br - 3CuSO₄ + 2PH₃ → Cu₃P + 2H₂SO₄ - 8AgNO₃ + PH₃ + 4H₂O → 8Ag + H₃PO₄ + 8HNO₃ - PH₃ + 2O₂ → H₃PO₄

rows.text: ***Holme's signal*** - a perforated container of CaC2 and Ca3P2 thrown overboard: seawater hydrolyses both to acetylene and phosphine, which ignite spontaneously - a red flame and smoke rising from the sea to call for help.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Phosphorus's Answer to Ammonia PH₃ (phosphine): prepared from phosphides, weakly basic, strongly reducing, and famous for spontaneous flammability from trace P₂H₄. Preparation, properties, action with halogens and oxygen, uses.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Preparation - **Lab:** white P + concentrated NaOH solution (in inert atmosphere, H₂ evolved): **P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂** (sodium hypophosphite). - From metal phosphides: **Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃** (carbide-style hydrolysis). - Pure PH₃: heat phosphonium iodide with NaOH: **PH₄I + NaOH → PH₃ + NaI + H₂O**.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Prep: P4 + NaOH -> PH3 + NaH2PO2. Angle 93.6 deg, dipole 0.58 D. CuSO4 gives Cu3P (not Cu!); AgNO3 gives Ag. Burns to H3PO4. PH4X with HX. P2H4 = self-igniter. Holme's signal = CaC2 + Ca3P2.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): How is phosphine prepared in the laboratory? Why is the gas spontaneously flammable?** — **Preparation:** white phosphorus is heated with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution in an **inert atmosphere** (hydrogen or CO₂, to exclude air): **P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂**.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Compare the basic character of NH3 and PH3 with reasons.** — **NH₃ is strongly basic**: the nitrogen lone pair is compact and tightly held, protonation to NH₄⁺ is easy, and ammonium hydroxide exists in water.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The CuSO4 trick question: write Cu3P (copper phosphide) - examiners set this trap every year; AgNO3 is the metal-mirror case.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Down group 15 the lone pair weakens: NH3 donates eagerly (stable NH4OH, 107 deg, H-bonded) while PH3 barely donates (PH4+ only with strong acids, 93.6 deg, no H-bonding, bp -87.7 C) - basicity and hydrogen bonding die together down the group.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: PH3 prep: P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O -> PH3 + 3NaH2PO2 (conc NaOH, inert atmosphere); Ca3P2 + 6H2O -> 3Ca(OH)2 + 2PH3; pure from PH4I + NaOH. Impure gas has P2H4 -> spontaneously flammable (vortex rings).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Phosphine is used as a dopant gas in the semiconductor industry - the garlic-smelling poison helps build every silicon chip.

Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why PH₃ is a weak base compared to NH₃ - Phosphorus is larger, less electronegative; its lone pair is diffuse and poorly held. Protonation is unfavourable; PH₄⁺ exists only with strong acids. Also no hydrogen bonding: PH₃ boils at −87.7 °C, far below NH₃'s −33 °C despite being heavier — the H-bonding absence is visible in the boiling point.…  ·  ## 5.
